summary: Specifies a key exchange based on discrete logarithm cryptography that is authenticated with a password or passphrase. It resists active attack, passive attack and offline dictionary attack. It comes from the Crypto Forum Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: Dragonfly lets two people who already share a password agree on a shared secret key without putting the password, or anything derived from it, on the network. The exchange takes two rounds of messages. An attacker who only records the traffic cannot check password guesses offline, so a captured recording cannot be used to search a word list.

what is a password-authenticated key exchange
how does dragonfly resist dictionary attacks
subtitle: A password-based key exchange that leaves an eavesdropper no password guess to test offline.

tldr.problem: Passwords are the main way people authenticate on the Internet, but protocols that send password-derived data let anyone who records one exchange check a whole word list against it later, without the server.
tldr.mechanism: Both peers turn the password into one secret element inside a chosen cryptographic group, commit to a guess of it in a first exchange, confirm it in a second, and stretch the agreed secret into a key confirmation key and a master key.
tldr.outcome: The exchange resists active attack, passive attack and offline dictionary attack, and it produces an authenticated shared key that another protocol such as IPsec can use to protect data.

today: RFC 7664 is an Informational document published in November 2015 as a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group of the IRTF. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it is a research result rather than an Internet Standard.

sections.title: Why Passwords Need a Stronger Exchange
sections.content:
Passwords and passphrases are the predominant way of doing authentication on the Internet today. Many protocols that use them exchange password-derived data as a proof that the sender knows the password, for example RFC 7296 (IKEv2) and RFC 5433 (EAP-GPSK).

That arrangement has a weakness. If an attacker gathers enough from an exchange, whether by listening in or by taking part in it, the recorded data can be checked against a pool of candidate passwords without any further interaction. Each candidate is turned into the same password-derived data and compared. This is an offline dictionary attack.

Dragonfly is built so that an attacker cannot do that. The RFC defines resistance to dictionary attack this way: any advantage the adversary gains must come directly from the number of interactions she has with an honest participant, and not from computation. The adversary obtains no information about the password except whether a single guess in a single run was correct or not.

Both peers hold an identical copy of the password and both agree on the same set of domain parameters, which the document calls a group. Because the two sides are treated the same way, Dragonfly works in traditional client-server protocols and also in peer-to-peer applications with no fixed roles, where either party may start the exchange and both may implement it at the same time.
sections.plainLanguage: Many protocols prove that a user knows a password by sending something computed from it. Anyone who records that exchange can test a word list against it later, with no help from the server. Dragonfly removes that shortcut: a recorded run reveals only whether one guess was right or wrong.

sections.title: The Groups Dragonfly Uses
sections.content:
Dragonfly uses discrete logarithm cryptography for authentication and key agreement. Each party derives ephemeral keys with respect to a set of domain parameters, called a group. A group is based either on finite field cryptography (FFC) or on elliptic curve cryptography (ECC).

Three operations are defined for both kinds of group. The scalar operation takes a scalar and an element and produces another element. The element operation takes two elements and produces a third. The inverse operation takes an element and returns another element such that combining the two with the element operation produces the identity element of the group.

In an ECC group the element operation is addition of points on an elliptic curve. The scalar operation multiplies a point by a number, and the inverse operation finds the point that adds up to the point at infinity. The domain parameters are a prime p that determines the field, the coefficients a and b that define the curve equation, a generator point G whose order is a sufficiently large prime, and a prime q that is the order of G and the size of the subgroup it generates. An ECC group used with Dragonfly MUST have a cofactor of one.

In an FFC group the element operation is multiplication modulo p. The scalar operation raises an element to a power modulo p, and the inverse operation finds the value that multiplies back to one. The domain parameters are a prime p, a generator G whose multiplicative order is a sufficiently large prime divisor of (p-1)/2, and a prime q that is the order of G. A valid FFC element lies strictly between 1 and p-1 and, raised to the power q, comes back to one modulo p.
sections.plainLanguage: Dragonfly does its arithmetic inside a group: a set of values with rules for combining them. The rules differ between elliptic curves and finite fields, but the document uses the same three operations for both, so the exchange works the same way either way.

sections.title: Turning the Password into a Secret Element
sections.content:
Before any information is exchanged, the peers MUST derive a secret element in the chosen group, called the Password Element (PE). From the point of view of an attacker who does not know the password, the PE is a random element of the negotiated group.

The derivation starts from a secret seed and a group-specific search loop. A security parameter k is used so that at least k iterations are always performed, which hides how many iterations the loop actually needed. The probability that more than n iterations are required is roughly (q/2p)^n for an ECC group and roughly (q/p)^n for an FFC group, and both drop quickly as n grows.

Each iteration starts from an 8-bit counter set to one and computes a base by hashing the two identities in a fixed order, the password and the counter: base = H(max(Alice,Bob) | min(Alice,Bob) | password | counter). Passing the identities through the maximum and minimum functions gives the hash a fixed ordering while still letting either side see itself as the initiator. The base is stretched with a key derivation function to a length of len(p) + 64 bits and reduced modulo (p - 1) to produce the seed. The extra 64 bits are there so that the bias from the modular reduction is not so apparent.

With an ECC group, the seed is tried as an x-coordinate and the curve equation is checked to see whether x^3 + a*x + b is a quadratic residue modulo p. If it is not, the counter is incremented and a new base and seed are generated. When it is, the y-coordinate is solved for, and the low-order bit of the stored base picks between the two possible values of y. With an FFC group, the seed is raised to the power (p-1)/q modulo p, and the result becomes the PE if it is greater than one.

The document notes that checking whether a value is a quadratic residue can leak information through a side channel, so it recommends blinding the value with a random number before the check. If the surrounding protocol can exchange random nonces, the RFC says they SHOULD be added to the base computation so that each run of the protocol produces a different PE.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides turn the password into one secret value inside the chosen group before they talk. They do it the same way: hash the password with a counter and repeat until the result is a valid value in the group. The loop always runs a fixed minimum number of times, so the time it takes gives nothing away.

sections.title: The Commit Exchange and the Confirm Exchange
sections.content:
The exchange has two parts. In the Commit Exchange both sides commit to a single guess of the password. In the Confirm Exchange both sides confirm that they derived the same secret and therefore hold the same password.

For the commit, each peer generates two random numbers, private and mask, each greater than one and less than the group order q. These two secrets and the Password Element produce the values that are sent: scalar = (private + mask) modulo q and Element = inverse(scalar-op(mask, PE)). If the scalar is less than two, the private and mask values MUST be thrown away and new ones generated. Once a valid scalar and element exist, the mask is no longer needed and MUST be irretrievably destroyed.

The peers exchange their scalar and element. If the peer's values are identical to the local ones, that is a sign of a reflection attack and the exchange MUST be aborted. Otherwise the peer-scalar MUST be between 1 and q, exclusive, and the Peer-Element must pass the validation rules of the group in use. If either check fails, the exchange MUST be terminated and authentication fails. If both pass, the shared secret is computed as ss = F(scalar-op(private, element-op(peer-Element, scalar-op(peer-scalar, PE)))).

To enforce key separation, the shared secret is stretched into two subkeys, a key confirmation key and a master key, using kck | mk = KDF-n(ss, label) where the label is the string Dragonfly Key Derivation and n = len(p)*2. Each subkey SHOULD be at least the length of the prime used in the selected group.

For the confirm, each side computes confirm = H(kck | scalar | peer-scalar | Element | Peer-Element | sender-id), with the scalars before the elements and the sender's value before the recipient's. The sender identity is the one the sender contributed to the base in Section 3.2. The two peers exchange these confirmations and check the correctness of the one they receive. If the peer's confirmation is valid, authentication succeeds; if it is not valid, authentication fails. On failure, all ephemeral state created during that run MUST be irretrievably destroyed. On success, the master key can be exported as an authenticated and secret key for another protocol to use, for instance IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides each send a number built from their own secret and from the password element. Each side then works out the same shared secret from what it sent and what it received. A final exchange of hashes of that secret tells each side whether the other one holds the same password.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The exchange requires both participants to have an identical representation of the password. Salting does not change that: the salted password simply becomes the credential that both sides must hold identically. If an adversary gains access to a database of salted passwords, she can impersonate one side to the other even though she cannot determine the underlying, unsalted password.

Resistance to dictionary attack means the adversary must launch an active attack to make a single guess at the password. If the dictionary has d entries and each is equally likely to be the shared password, then one guess succeeds with probability 1/d. After x guesses, with the failed ones removed from the pool, the probability becomes 1/(d-x), so it grows as x grows. Repeated guessing therefore does work over time. Users SHOULD ensure that the size of the pool the password was drawn from is large enough to make this attack preventable, and implementations SHOULD support countermeasures, such as refusing authentication attempts for a certain amount of time once the number of failed attempts reaches a threshold. The memo recommends no threshold and no amount of time.

Groups that contain a small subgroup cause problems, so it is RECOMMENDED that implementations not allow a group's complete domain parameters to be sent in-line. Instead they should use a common repository and pass an identifier for a domain parameter set whose strength has been rigorously proven and that has no small subgroups. If a complete parameter set is sent in-line, it SHOULD NOT be used with Dragonfly unless it directly matches a known good group.

The document RECOMMENDS setting the security parameter k to a value of at least forty, which puts the probability of needing more than forty iterations at about one in one trillion. The technique used to obtain the Password Element was viewed as controversial by some reviewers in the Crypto Forum Research Group, and an alternate method such as the one in hash2ec can be used instead. The protocol has received cryptanalysis in the IET Information Security paper listed below, and a security proof in the random oracle model is given for the case where both identities are included in the data sent in the Confirm Exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: Salted passwords do not protect a server that stores them, because both sides still need the same copy of the salted value. An attacker can also keep guessing one password at a time over the network, so the pool of possible passwords should be large. The document recommends refusing attempts for a while after repeated failures.

items.text: The exchange resists an adversary who takes part in it.

items.title: Passive attack

items.title: Offline dictionary attack

data.title: Fixing the Password Element for an ECC group
data.code:
found = 0
counter = 1
n = len(p) + 64
do {
  base = H(max(Alice,Bob) | min(Alice,Bob) | password | counter)
  temp = KDF-n(base, "Dragonfly Hunting And Pecking")
  seed = (temp mod (p - 1)) + 1
  if ( (seed^3 + a*seed + b) is a quadratic residue mod p)
  then
    if ( found == 0 )
    then
      x = seed
      save = base
      found = 1
    fi
  fi
  counter = counter + 1
} while ((found == 0) || (counter <= k))
y = sqrt(x^3 + ax + b)
if ( lsb(y) == lsb(save) )
then
  PE = (x,y)
else
  PE = (x,p-y)
fi
